read.sections.1.text.back: People all over the world use art to tell stories and store knowledge. At Tassili n'Ajjer, Algeria, paintings on rock show hippos and herds of cattle. Now that area is desert, so the pictures tell us that the Sahara used to be much greener. In China, there is a scroll painting more than five metres long. The painting shows more than 800 people shopping, travelling, and working in a busy city about 900 years ago. Its title is Along the River during the Qingming Festival. In Vanuatu, in the Pacific, sand drawers use one finger to draw one long line. Their drawings help people remember stories and knowledge.
read.sections.1.text.source: People around the world use art to tell stories and keep knowledge. At Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria, rock art shows hippos and herds of cattle. The land there is desert today, so the pictures tell us the Sahara was once much greener. In China, there is a painted scroll more than five metres long. It shows over 800 people shopping, travelling and working in a busy city about 900 years ago. It is called Along the River During the Qingming Festival. In Vanuatu, in the Pacific, sand drawers use one finger to draw one long line. Their drawings help people remember stories and knowledge.

watch.summary.back: This is the same short video from Lesson 15. This video is from the Ayala Museum in the Philippines. This time, pay close attention to the details. The video shows a small green pot from China with two dragons on it. The video also shows a salakot, a wide woven hat, decorated with shells and silver. There is also a small piece of cloth with a poem sewn on it. Each detail is a clue. The dragons make the pot unusual, because most pots like that are plain. The shells and silver hint that the hat's owner was an important person. The poem tells us the feelings of the cloth's owner. A careful observer first says what they see. Then they say what it roughly means, and which detail supports that idea.
watch.summary.source: This is the same short video from Lesson 15. It comes from the Ayala Museum in the Philippines. This time, watch closely for details. The video shows a small green pot from China with two dragons on it. It shows a salakot, a wide woven hat, decorated with shell and silver. It also shows a small cloth with a poem sewn into it. Each detail is a clue. The dragons make the pot unusual, because most pots like it were plain. The shell and silver suggest that an important person owned the hat. The poem tells us how the cloth's owner felt. A careful viewer first says what they see. Then they say what it might mean, and which details support that idea.

read.sections.0.heading.back: Start from what you can see
read.sections.0.heading.source: Start with what you can see

read.sections.0.text.back: When looking at an artwork, start from what you can see. Name the colours, people, objects, and words that are there. Pay attention to the composition, that is, the way the parts of the picture are arranged. In the poster, a blue river flows in the middle. Three people carry buckets towards one tap, and a child points at a cracked pipe. All of these are observations. Observations are facts anyone can check by looking. The words "Water for every street" are also part of the evidence. Only after looking carefully do you decide what the artwork roughly means.
read.sections.0.text.source: When you look at an artwork, begin with what you can see. Name the colours, people, objects and any words. Notice the composition, which means how the parts are arranged. In the poster, a blue river runs through the centre. Three people carry buckets towards one tap, and a child points at a cracked pipe. These are observations. They are facts that anyone can check by looking. The words “Water for every street” are also part of the evidence. Only after you look closely should you decide what the artwork might mean.

The words on the poster are also evidence. Look carefully first. Then think about the meaning.

read.sections.1.heading.back: Art has told stories for a very long time
read.sections.1.heading.source: Art has told stories for a very long time

read.sections.1.simpler.back: People all over the world tell stories through art. In Algeria, there are old paintings on rock. The paintings show cattle and river animals. Now the land is desert. So, the paintings tell us that the land used to be green. In China, there is a long scroll painting. The painting shows a busy city. There are more than 800 people in it. They shop, work, and travel. In Vanuatu, people draw in sand with one finger. The drawing helps them remember stories.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: People all over the world tell stories with art. In Algeria, old rock art shows cows and river animals. Now the land is desert. So the art tells us the land was once green. In China, a long painted scroll shows a busy city. It shows more than 800 people. They shop, work and travel. In Vanuatu, people draw in the sand with one finger. The drawings help them remember stories.

read.sections.2.text.back: An interpretation is an idea about what an artwork means. A strong interpretation points to details. Observer 1 thinks the poster is about people who don't have enough water. The line of people at one tap and the words at the bottom support this idea. Observer 2 thinks the poster is asking the city to fix pipes, because the child points right at that pipe. Both ideas use evidence, so both can make sense. It also helps if you think about the audience, that is, the people the artist wants to reach. Words like "maybe" and "could be" show that you are being careful.
read.sections.2.text.source: An interpretation is an idea about what an artwork means. A strong interpretation points to details. Viewer 1 thinks the poster is about people who do not have enough water. The line of people at one tap and the words at the bottom support this idea. Viewer 2 thinks the poster asks the town to fix the pipe, because the child points right at it. Both ideas use evidence, so both can make sense. It also helps to think about the audience, the people the artist wanted to reach. Words like “may” and “might” show that you are being careful.

read.sections.2.simpler.back: An interpretation is an idea about what an artwork means. A good interpretation points to details. Observer 1 thinks some people lack water. Many people wait at one tap. That is a clue. Observer 2 thinks the poster asks the city to fix pipes. The child points at that pipe. Both ideas use evidence. Think also about the poster's audience. Who does the artist want to see the poster? Use words like "maybe" and "could be".
